source_text: Paulus vero Apostolus de persecutore, qui primus Ecclesiae sanguinem fudit, postea gladium stylo mutans, et convertens machaeram in aratrum; lupus rapax Benjamin, dehinc ipse afferens escam secundum Jacob, qualiter martyria, jam et sibi optabilia, commendat! cum de Thessalonicensibus gaudens: Uti, inquit, gloriemur in vobis in Ecclesiis Dei pro tolerantia vestra et fide, in omnibus persecutionibus et pressuris, quibus sustinetis ostentamen justi judicii Dei, ut digni habeamini regno ejus, pro quo et patimini. Sicut et ad Romanos: Non solum autem, verum etiam exultantes in pressuris; certi quod pressura tolerantiam perficit, tolerantia vero probationem, probatio autem spem, spes vero non confundit. Et rursus: Quod si filii, et haeredes; haeredes quidem Dei, cohaeredes vero Christi: siquidem compatimur, uti et cum illo glorificemur. Reputo enim passiones hujus temporis non esse dignas ad gloriam, quae in nobis revelabitur. Et ideo postmodum: Quis, inquit, separabit nos a dilectione Christi? pressura, an angustia, an fames, an nuditas, an periculum, an machaera, secundum quod scriptum est: tui caussa mortificamur tota die, deputati sumus ut pecora jugulationis; sed in omnibus istis supervincimus pro eo qui nos dilexit. Persuasum enim habemus, quod neque mors, neque vita, neque virtus, neque sublimitas, neque profundum, neque alia conditio poterit nos a dilectione Dei separare, quae est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro. Sed et Corinthiis passiones suas enumerans, patiendum utique praefinivit: In laboribus abundantius, in carceribus plurimum, in mortibus saepius; a Judaeis quinquies quadragenas citra unam accepi, ter virgis caesus, semel lapidatus, et reliqua. Quae si magis incommoda quam martyria videbuntur, tamen rursus: Propter quod, inquit, boni duco in infirmitatibus, in injuriis, in necessitatibus, in persecutionibus, in angustiis pro Christo. Etiam in superioribus: Qui in omnibus tribulemur, sed non coangustemur; et indigeamus, sed non perindigeamus; quoniam persecutionibus agitemur, sed non derelinquamur; qui dejiciamur, sed non pereamus: semper mortificationem Christi Jesu in corpore nostro circumferentes. Sed etsi, inquit, exterior homo noster vitiatur, caro scilicet, vi persecutionum; sed interior renovatur die et die; anima scilicet spe promissionum. Nam quod ad praesens, temporale et leve pressurae nostrae per supergressum in supergressum aeternum pondus gloriae perficit nobis, non intuentibus quae videntur, sed quae non videntur. Quae enim videntur, temporalia, de incommodis dicens; quae vero non videntur, aeterna, de praemiis spondens. Thessalonicensibus vero de vinculis scribens, utique beatos affirmavit,, quibus donatum esset non tantum credere in Christum, sed etiam pro ipso pati: Eumdem, inquit, agonem habentes quem in me vidistis, et nunc audistis. Nam et si libor super sacrificium, gaudeo et congaudeo omnibus vobis, perinde et vos gaudete et congaudete mihi. Vides quam martyrii definiat felicitatem, cui de gaudio mutuo acquirit solemnitatem. Ut proximus denique voti sui factus est, qualiter de prospectu ejus exsultans Timotheo scribit? Ego enim jam libor, et tempus dijunctionis instat. Agonem bonum decertavi, cursum consummavi, fidem custodivi; superest corona, quam mihi Dominus illa die reddet, scilicet passionis. Satis et ipse supra allocutus: Fidelis sermo: si enim commortui sumus Christo, et convivemus; si sufferimus, et conregnabimus; si negaverimus, et ille nos negabit; si non credimus, ille fidelis est, negare se non potest. Ne ergo confundaris martyrio Domini nostri, neque me vinctum ejus; quia praedixerat: Non enim dedit nobis Deus spiritum timoris, sed virtutis et dilectionis et sanae mentis. Virtute enim patimur ex dilectione in Deum, et sana mente, cum ob innocentiam patimur. Sed et sicubi tolerantiam praecipit, quibus magis eam quam passionibus prospicit? sicubi ab idololatria divellit, quid ei magis quam martyria praevellit?
pass_a_gloss: Paul, indeed, an Apostle, concerning a persecutor, who first shed the Church's blood, afterwards changing the sword for a stylus, and converting the sword into a plow; a rapacious wolf of Benjamin, thereafter himself bringing food, according to Jacob, in what way he commends martyrdoms, now already desirable to himself! when rejoicing about the Thessalonians: We glory, he says, in you in the Churches of God for your endurance and faith, in all the persecutions and pressures which you endure, a demonstration of the just judgment of God, so that you may be considered worthy of His kingdom, for which you also suffer. Just as also to the Romans: Not only, indeed, but also rejoicing in pressures; certain that pressure perfects endurance, endurance, indeed, testing, testing, indeed, hope, hope, indeed, does not disappoint. And again: If we are sons, and heirs; heirs, indeed, of God, but co-heirs of Christ: if, indeed, we suffer, so that we may also be glorified with Him. I consider, indeed, the sufferings of this time not to be worthy of the glory which will be revealed in us. And therefore afterwards: Who, he says, will separate us from the love of Christ? pressure, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or sword, according to what has been written: for Your sake we are killed all day, we have been considered as sheep for slaughter; but in all these things we overcome on account of Him who loved us. For we are persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor virtue, nor height, nor depth, nor any other condition will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. But also to the Corinthians, enumerating his own sufferings, he has predetermined that we must suffer: In labors more abundantly, in prisons more frequently, in deaths often; from the Jews I received forty lashes minus one five times, three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, and the rest. Which, if they seem more inconveniences than martyrdoms, nevertheless again: On account of which, he says, I consider it good in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ. Also in the preceding words: Who in all things are troubled, but not constrained; and we are in need, but not in extreme need; since we are persecuted, but not abandoned; who are cast down, but not perishing: always carrying the mortification of Christ Jesus in our body. But if, he says, our outer man is being destroyed, namely, the flesh, by the power of persecutions; but the inner man is being renewed day by day; namely, the soul by the hope of promises. For what is present, temporal, and light, our pressure, through surpassing, surpasses into eternal weight of glory, not looking at what is seen, but at what is not seen. For what is seen is temporal, speaking of inconveniences; what, indeed, is not seen, is eternal, promising rewards. To the Thessalonians, indeed, writing about his chains, he has affirmed, indeed, blessed are those to whom it has been given not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for Him: Having, he says, the same struggle which you saw in me and now hear. For even if I am poured out as a sacrifice, I rejoice and congratulate all of you, and you, in turn, rejoice and congratulate me. You see how he defines the happiness of martyrdom, acquiring solemnity from mutual joy. So that, finally, having become near to his own wish, he writes to Timothy, exulting from his own prospect? For I am already being poured out, and the time of departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; there remains a crown, which the Lord will give me on that day, namely, of passion. Having spoken sufficiently above: Faithful is the word: if, indeed, we have died with Christ, and we live; if we suffer, and we will reign; if we deny, and He will deny us; if we do not believe, He is faithful, He cannot deny Himself. So do not be ashamed of the martyrdom of our Lord, nor of me, bound for Him; because He has foretold: For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, and love, and a sound mind. For we suffer with power from love for God, and with a sound mind, when we suffer for innocence. But also where he commands endurance, to whom does he foresee it more than for martyrdoms? where he tears away from idolatry, what does he tear away more than martyrdoms?

pass_b_english: Paul the Apostle — once a persecutor who spilled the Church's first blood, then trading his sword for a pen and beating his blade into a plowshare; the ravening wolf of Benjamin who ends up bringing food, as Jacob said — how he commends martyrdoms, now desirable even to himself! Rejoicing over the Thessalonians he writes: we boast of you in the churches of God for your endurance and faith in all the persecutions and pressures you endure, a demonstration of God's just judgment, so that you may be counted worthy of his kingdom, for which you also suffer (2 Thess 1:4-5). Just as he tells the Romans: not only that, but we even exult in pressures, knowing that pressure produces endurance, endurance produces character, character produces hope, and hope does not disappoint (Rom 5:3-5). And again: if we are children, then we are heirs — heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ — provided we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him (Rom 8:17). For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed in us (Rom 8:18). And so he goes on: Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Pressure, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? As it is written: "For your sake we are being killed all day long; we were regarded as sheep for slaughter." Yet in all these things we more than conquer through him who loved us (Rom 8:35-37). For I am persuaded that neither death nor life nor angels nor rulers nor things present nor things to come nor powers nor height nor depth nor anything else in all creation will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord (Rom 8:38-39).

To the Corinthians, cataloguing his own sufferings, he insists that suffering is the lot: in labors more abundantly, in imprisonments more frequently, in deaths often; five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one, three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, and the rest (2 Cor 11:23-25). If these seem more like hardships than martyrdoms, still he says again: therefore I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities for Christ's sake (2 Cor 12:10). Also earlier: we are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed; always carrying in the body the death of Jesus (2 Cor 4:8-10). For even if our outer self is wasting away — the flesh, by the force of persecutions — yet our inner self is being renewed day by day — the soul, by the hope of promises (2 Cor 4:16). For this slight momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison, as we look not to what is seen but to what is unseen; for what is seen is transient, but what is unseen is eternal (2 Cor 4:17-18). Writing to the Thessalonians about his chains, he declares blessed those to whom it has been granted not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for him: having the same conflict which you saw in me and now hear to be in me (Phil 1:29-30). For even if I am poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrifice of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with you all; likewise you also should be glad and rejoice with me (Phil 2:17-18). You see how he defines the happiness of martyrdom, drawing its solemnity from mutual joy.

So at last, nearing his own desire, he writes to Timothy exulting in his prospect: For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure has come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that Day (2 Tim 4:6-8). Having said enough above: the saying is trustworthy: If we have died with him, we will also live with him; if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he also will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful — for he cannot deny himself (2 Tim 2:11-13). Do not therefore be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, nor of me his prisoner; for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control (2 Tim 1:8, 7). For we suffer by power from love for God, and with a sound mind, when we suffer for innocence. But where does he command endurance, foreseeing it for whom more than for martyrs? Where does he tear men from idolatry, tearing them toward what more than toward martyrdoms?

review.notes: Pass B fails on several counts of agency, doctrine, and completeness relative to the Locked Latin. 1. Agency/Completeness: In the section regarding the crown, Pass B adds 'of righteousness' and 'the righteous judge' which are not in the Latin 'superest corona, quam mihi Dominus illa die reddet'. 2. Doctrine/Completeness: In the section regarding Romans 8:38-39, Pass B adds a massive amount of content ('nor angels nor rulers nor things present nor things to come nor powers nor anything else in all creation') that is entirely absent from the Locked Latin 'neque mors, neque vita, neque virtus, neque sublimitas, neque profundum, neque alia conditio'. 3. Agency: In the final sentence, Pass B translates 'quid ei magis quam martyria praevellit?' as 'Where does he tear men from idolatry, tearing them toward what more than toward martyrdoms?', which introduces 'men' and changes the direction/object of the action compared to the Latin.
reasons: Pass B adds significant content to the Romans 8:38-39 passage ('nor angels nor rulers nor things present nor things to come nor powers nor anything else in all creation') not present in the Locked Latin ('neque mors, neque vita, neque virtus, neque sublimitas, neque profundum, neque alia conditio').
Pass B adds 'of righteousness' and 'the righteous judge' to the description of the crown, which is not in the Latin ('superest corona, quam mihi Dominus illa die reddet').
Pass B introduces 'men' in the final sentence ('Where does he tear men from idolatry') which is not in the Latin ('sicubi ab idololatria divellit').
